one_line: Leak/freeze sensors, boiler-and-heat monitoring, and local camera analytics for independent multifamily owners and small property managers in Middlesex County - sold as a monitored installation, not a SaaS subscription.

problem.summary: Small, independently owned multifamily portfolios (garden apartments, 3-40 unit buildings, mixed-use strips) are run by a handful of people with no building automation. Water damage and freezing is the second-largest cause of homeowners loss after wind and hail (22.6% of 2023 losses), heat failures in winter are a regulated habitability issue in New Jersey with a specific 68F/65F standard, package and parking incidents generate tenant complaints, and every one of these is discovered by a tenant phone call rather than by the building. Existing enterprise proptech (Sensor Industries, Alert Labs, Runwise, Verkada, Rhombus) prices per unit or per camera with ongoing licenses that assume many units or several hundred dollars of camera hardware per location, so the 20-200 unit owner is left doing rounds with a clipboard and a key ring. (Inference: the per-unit and per-camera price points documented below are what make this segment hard to serve with those products.)

evidence.fact: Water damage and freezing accounted for 22.6% of homeowners insurance losses incurred in 2023 and 25.8% in 2022 - the second-largest cause of loss after wind and hail.

Average severity of a water-damage-and-freezing claim was $15,400 (weighted average 2019-2023), with claim frequency of 1.50 per 100 house-years - i.e. roughly 1.5% of insured dwellings file a water claim every year.

Gallagher's real-estate claims review is reported to put the average incurred water-damage claim on its commercial real-estate book at $55,045 for claims from January 2019 to January 2021. UNVERIFIED: the report page would not render for me in two separate sessions; the figure comes from a search-index summary, not from a page I read. No multifamily-specific severity figure was confirmed anywhere.
evidence.year: 2021 claim period (report undated in what I could see)

evidence.fact: New Jersey requires every apartment and habitable room to be held at 68F from 6am-11pm and 65F from 11pm-6am between October 1 and May 15, and makes the owner responsible for maintaining the heating system in good operating condition regardless of contract language.
At least 58 million packages were stolen in the US in 2024 with as much as $16 billion in financial losses, per the USPS Office of Inspector General.

NJ DCA's Truth in Renting states that a landlord generally has no right to enter a rented dwelling without the tenant's consent or a Superior Court judgment, and that entering while the tenant is away without permission is forcible entry under N.J.S.A. 2A:39-2. The same document states that, under N.J.A.C. 5:10-1.2, upon reasonable notification tenants must give the landlord and the landlord's employees access to the unit for inspection and maintenance, with reasonable notification normally one day (immediate access in a safety or structural emergency); consent of the tenant is separately required for inspection of the private living quarters except in emergencies or where access has been denied (N.J.A.C. 5:10-1.10(d)). So an in-unit sensor install turns on lease language plus notice rather than a signed consent in every case, and anything beyond inspection/maintenance needs its own lease provision.
evidence.year: 2024 edition of NJ DCA Truth in Renting

evidence.fact: Property, real estate and community association managers (SOC 11-9141) earn a median $82,850 in New Jersey and $96,950 in the New York-Newark-Jersey City metro (BLS May 2025 wage data). At that loaded cost, an hour of manual rounds or after-hours leak response is roughly $40-50/hr fully loaded (inference: median annual wage / 2,080 hours plus ~30% burden), which is the baseline any monitoring service has to beat.
evidence.year: 2026 release of May 2025 BLS OEWS data

buyers.business_type: Owner-operators of garden apartments and small walk-ups (own the building, self-manage or use a part-time super)
buyers.size_where_it_matters: 20-200 units, or 3+ buildings; the pain starts when the owner can no longer personally walk every basement and boiler room weekly. Buildings with 3+ units are 'multiple dwellings' under NJ DCA rules and carry registration/inspection obligations.
buyers.why: They eat the deductible and the uninsured portion of every water loss, pay the heat bill, and answer the 2am phone call themselves. No IT staff, so a turnkey installed system is the only realistic purchase.

buyers.business_type: Independent residential property management companies (manage for other owners, collect a per-unit fee)
buyers.size_where_it_matters: 5-50 staff managing roughly 500-5,000 units across 20-150 buildings; below ~300 units there is no maintenance director to absorb the work.
buyers.why: Monitoring is a defensible differentiator in management contract pitches and a way to reduce emergency calls per property manager. They can resell the service per unit and are the single best channel partner - one contract covers many buildings.

buyers.business_type: Small commercial / mixed-use property managers and strip-center owners
buyers.size_where_it_matters: 3-30 properties, 20,000-300,000 sq ft total; matters once they have multiple tenant spaces and shared restrooms/risers.
buyers.why: Same leak and after-hours problems, plus parking-lot and dumpster issues, but no on-site staff at night and lease clauses that make the landlord liable for certain systems.

buyers.size_where_it_matters: 1-5 facilities, 300-2,000 units; matters as soon as there is one gate and one camera system to maintain.
buyers.why: Cameras, gate/LPR and roof or sprinkler leaks over stored tenant property; highest loss-per-incident of the group because a single roof leak damages many units.

buyers.business_type: Independent limited-service hotels/motels and small assisted-living or group homes
buyers.size_where_it_matters: 20-120 rooms/beds with 5-40 staff; matters when there is a boiler, a commercial laundry, and no overnight maintenance tech.
buyers.why: Guest/tenant safety obligations, boiler and hot-water failures, and package/entry control; they already buy life-safety service contracts, so a monitored sensor add-on fits the buying pattern.

existing_solutions.pricing: Public example: 349-unit co-op paid $14,375/yr for monitoring, controls, software, support and internet, with $14,722 installation after a $10,578 utility rebate (2024)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Building controls plus remote operators who tune boilers and HVAC; markets guaranteed utility savings.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown (project quote; company advertises 20-30% utility savings - vendor claim, Low)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Plug-and-play PoE cameras with cloud video, people/vehicle analytics, and optional license plate recognition; popular with multifamily operators.
existing_solutions.pricing: CD22 indoor dome $799 MSRP; the price page states 'Price includes hardware. Additional license required' on every camera SKU and publishes no license price (license price not published; resellers quote per device)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Cloud-managed cameras with AI search, occupancy and alerting; sold through authorized resellers with published MSRP list prices and a per-camera license.
existing_solutions.pricing: Camera $399 (R120) to $3,299 (R600); license $149/camera (Professional tier) on the single-sensor SKUs, $649 on the R600 multisensor. R600 total $3,948. R200 $599 + $149 = $748 total. The page states 'AI-features and cloud archiving not included in the Professional License' (Enterprise tier on request), so the $748 anchor is a video/cloud-storage price, not an AI-analytics price; the license term is not stated on the page

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Carrier-integrated smart lockers and package rooms for multifamily, with delivery logging and resident notification.

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Runs on a mini PC or Pi, detects people/vehicles/custom objects per zone, records locally, publishes MQTT events that Home Assistant turns into alerts and work orders; built-in license plate recognition.

gap_for_local_installer: The product category is crowded at the top (enterprise per-unit SaaS) and at the bottom (DIY Aqara/Frigate hobby kits). The unserved middle is a 20-200 unit owner in Middlesex County who wants someone local to design zones, pull cable, mount sensors, write the alert routing to the right super's phone, and answer the phone when it fires. That gap is service-shaped, not product-shaped: (1) mixing cheap commodity sensors with one paid, monitored layer; (2) retrofitting pre-1950 brick buildings where WiFi is unreliable and boiler rooms are undocumented; (3) integrating with whatever the owner already uses (Buildium/AppFolio/AppSheet work orders, a 15-year-old analog camera DVR); (4) local nuisance-alert tuning (laundry-room humidity, steam pipes, delivery drivers) that national vendors will not do remotely; (5) plain-language NJ-specific compliance artifacts - tenant notice for in-unit sensors under the N.J.A.C. 5:10-1.2 one-day notice rule, retention policy, and heat-log export for a DCA or municipal inspection. The defensibility is the install base and the service relationship, not the models, which are free and getting better.

technical_approach.established_pattern: Three parallel layers on one local hub, with a human-in-the-loop notification path. Layer 1 (water/freeze): battery Zigbee/ZWave/Sub-GHz leak and temperature sensors at risers, boiler room, laundry, water heater closets, and - under lease language plus proper notice - under sinks in a sample of units; a local gateway runs threshold and rate-of-change rules. Layer 2 (cameras): PoE IP cameras into an on-prem NVR (Frigate) doing person/vehicle detection on substreams, with polygon zones and cross-line rules per area (package room, dumpster, parking, rear door); plate recognition only where there is a documented need. Layer 3 (heat/boiler): temperature sensors on supply/return and in representative apartments, plus boiler run-time and burner status from a current switch, dry-contact relay or Modbus/BACnet read; rules detect 'boiler running and no temperature rise', 'no call for heat below 68F', and short-cycling. A small vision-language model runs only on the handful of events the detector escalates (e.g. 'is this a package or a trash bag on the loading dock', 'is that a person loitering at the bike rack') so the owner gets a sentence, not 40 thumbnails. All alerting goes out through one channel (SMS/app + email digest) with an escalation rule and an auditable log.

hardware.item: Aqara Water Leak Sensor (Zigbee, battery) - per wet location

Dahua/Hikvision-class 4MP PoE turret - exterior and common areas. Frigate's hardware guide recommends Dahua/Hikvision and explicitly warns that many users report issues with 4K-plus Reolink cameras ('best to stick with 5MP and lower for Reolink'), so the camera choice follows that guidance rather than a 4K model
hardware.approx_cost: $219.99 list for an EmpireTech-branded Dahua-OEM 4MP turret (IPC-T54IR-AS-S3) at a US reseller; other models/lenses vary

hardware.item: Beelink EQ13 (Intel N100, dual NIC) mini PC as Frigate host - Frigate's own recommendation, isolates cameras on a second NIC
hardware.approx_cost: About $200 (inference: typical N100 mini-PC street price; Frigate docs give the model, not a price)

hardware.item: Raspberry Pi AI HAT+ 13 TOPS (Hailo-8L) if going the Pi route
hardware.approx_cost: $70 list for the 13 TOPS model ($110 for 26 TOPS), plus Pi 5 and storage

hardware.item: Boiler/heat layer: Zigbee or LoRa temperature/humidity sensors at supply/return and in sample apartments, plus a dry-contact or Modbus gateway for burner run-time
hardware.approx_cost: Unknown for a specific bill of materials; comparable paid service benchmarks at $14,375/yr for 349 units (Runwise, 2024)

technical_approach.fine_tuning_needed: Mostly no. Person/vehicle detection, zone rules and leak thresholds are pre-trained or rule-based and cover most of the value on day one (inference). Fine-tuning (or few-shot prompting a 2-3B VLM) is only justified for site-specific classes: package pile vs trash bag on a specific dock, a specific boiler gauge face, a specific vestibule door left propped. Frigate's hardware guide is explicit that a better camera view matters more than more compute, which is the same lesson for every custom class.
technical_approach.data_needed: Per site: floor plan and riser diagram, boiler make/model and control type, 2-4 weeks of baseline temperature and (if available) water-bill data, 200-1,000 labeled frames per custom visual class captured from the installed cameras over 1-2 weeks, the lease provisions and tenant notice covering in-unit sensors, and the alert escalation list (who, in what order, at what hour).

measured_outcomes.finding: CCTV was associated with about a 13% reduction in crime in camera areas versus control areas (odds ratio 1.141, p<.001); the effect for violent crime alone was smaller and not statistically significant.

Combining both phases, LPR-equipped patrols checked 8-10 times more plates than manual checking, produced nearly 3 times as many hits for stolen vehicles and twice as many vehicle recoveries - a process outcome. Unexpectedly, manual plate checking by the specialised unit (but not its LPR scanning) was associated with less auto theft two weeks after the intervention than regular patrol, there was no evidence of displacement, and the study found no evidence that LPR patrol reduced auto theft.
measured_outcomes.sample: Randomized patrol experiment in one Arizona jurisdiction (117 routes)

measured_outcomes.finding: Atlantic City's fixed-ALPR expansion (cameras on every entrance and exit) did not reduce violent crime overall, but was associated with reductions in shootings, motor vehicle theft and property crime; authors note use may be siloed in investigative units rather than patrol. A caution against selling LPR as a general crime-reduction product.
measured_outcomes.sample: One city (Atlantic City, NJ), interrupted time-series plus process evaluation

measured_outcomes.finding: Mercy Housing's Decatur Place (106 units, Denver) installed toilet-leak detectors, baseboard flood sensors and a continuous main-meter monitor; water consumption fell by over 30% and savings were expected to exceed $10,000 a year. No installed cost or grant figures were confirmed - the DOE case-study page itself would not load, so this comes from a 2023 industry compilation that restates the DOE report.
measured_outcomes.year: 2023 compilation of a DOE Better Buildings report

measured_outcomes.finding: A 349-unit Queens co-op reported more than $40,000/year in energy savings against a $14,375/year monitoring fee, with $14,722 installation after a $10,578 utility rebate.

Sensor Industries reports a 394-sensor commercial deployment at $115,000 cost with $790,000 in annualized savings including remediation and insurance effects - a vendor number that bundles avoided catastrophic loss with routine savings.

legal_privacy.issue: Video cameras in common areas (lobby, hallway, laundry, parking, package room)
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Negative finding, not a rule: searches of the NJ statutes and secondary summaries turned up no New Jersey statute specifically regulating landlord cameras in common areas. That is an absence of evidence, not confirmation that none applies. The outer limit I could confirm is N.J.S.A. 2C:14-9, which criminalises observing or recording a person where they reasonably expect privacy and may expose intimate parts or engage in sexual activity. Bathrooms, changing areas and views into unit interiors are out.

N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-4(d) permits interception of an oral communication by a party to it or with one party's prior consent, but recording tenants' or employees' conversations without consent is risky and adds a wiretap claim to any dispute. Practical rule for this avenue: ship cameras with audio disabled.

legal_privacy.issue: Sensors and cameras inside a rented unit
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Truth in Renting states a landlord generally has no right to enter a rented dwelling without the tenant's consent or a Superior Court judgment, and entering while the tenant is away without permission is forcible entry under N.J.S.A. 2A:39-2. It also states that under N.J.A.C. 5:10-1.2 tenants must give the landlord and its employees access for inspection and maintenance upon reasonable notification, normally one day, with immediate access in a safety or structural emergency; tenant consent is separately required for inspecting the private living quarters except in emergencies or where access has been denied (N.J.A.C. 5:10-1.10(d)). Practical reading: an in-unit leak/temperature sensor install is a maintenance access covered by lease language plus one-day notice, not a fresh signed consent per unit - but anything beyond inspection/maintenance (e.g. cameras inside a unit) has no statutory access right and must be bargained for in the lease.

The New Jersey Data Privacy Act (P.L. 2023, c.266, N.J.S.A. 56:8-166.4 et seq.) took effect January 15, 2025. It treats biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person as sensitive data requiring consent, and defines biometric data to include facial templates - while excluding ordinary photographs and video unless data derived from them is used to identify someone.

A1494 would make it an unlawful practice for a business entity to use a 'biometric surveillance system' (facial recognition or other remote biometric recognition) on a consumer at its physical premises without clear and conspicuous notice and a lawful purpose, and would bar selling data so obtained. This is commercial/consumer use at premises, not employer monitoring of employees. I read the introduced bill text; I did not confirm final enactment status from the Legislature's status page.

legal_privacy.issue: Whether NJDPA thresholds reach a 100-unit landlord
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Not confirmed. I did not verify the controller applicability thresholds (revenue/consumer-volume tests) in the Act text, so I cannot state whether a small owner is covered; the safe posture is to treat in-unit biometrics as off the table and avoid face recognition entirely.

No New Jersey statute found requiring notice to employees for ordinary video-only workplace cameras; a separate rule covers tracking devices in employee vehicles. Union contracts, leases and municipal rules can add notice duties, and cameras must not be used to watch protected concerted activity.

Not confirmed - I found no NJ statute setting a retention period for private camera footage. Practical posture: 14-30 day rolling retention, written policy, no footage sharing except to police with a log entry, and no tenant-facing 'we will catch the thief' promise that the system cannot keep.

legal_privacy.issue: False accusation risk from automated detection or plate reads
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: Inference, no source: any alert that names a person or vehicle ('tenant in 4B left water running', 'unauthorized vehicle') creates defamation and fair-housing exposure if wrong. Detector output should be treated as a lead for a human to verify against a second frame or sensor, never as a finding, and plate reads should never be used to tow or fine without human review. I did not find a source that quantifies this exposure for private property managers.

public: Google/Yelp reviews of the management company that mention heat, hot water, leaks, mold, package theft or parking - specific complaint language is the strongest public signal.

NJ DCA / municipal code-enforcement or housing-inspection records and no-heat complaints (the DCA Bureau of Housing Inspection inspects multiple dwellings; complaints route through municipal code enforcement).
Building age and construction from public listings/assessor records: pre-1950 brick garden apartments with steam boilers and no central AC are the highest-fit retrofits.
Number of buildings and unit counts on the manager's own website or listing pages (portfolio size is the whole qualification: under ~20 units they will not pay, over ~300 they have a vendor).
Job posts for 'maintenance technician' or 'porter' that list 'on-call rotation', 'respond to water leaks', or 'boiler operator license' - a live signal that response is manual and painful.
Whether the property already advertises 'smart locks', 'package lockers' or '24/7 maintenance' - an owner already buying amenity tech is pre-qualified.
Owners of small commercial strips with shared restrooms and flat roofs (leak-prone) visible on Street View.
Insurance renewal timing: ask when their policy renews; a broker conversation about water deductibles or a premium increase is the best-timed pitch.
walk_in: Boiler room: single steam boiler, manual gauge glass, no low-water cutoff log, cardboard boxes stored next to the burner, no temperature sensors or modem.
Basement/crawl: water stains on joists, a dehumidifier running, a sump pump with no alarm, copper supply lines with old shutoffs and no main shutoff valve that the super can find in 30 seconds.
Laundry room: no leak pan under washers, no floor drain, humidity peeling paint - a cheap first sensor cluster that demos well.
Front vestibule: packages stacked on the floor with no locker or camera, or a camera that is visibly unplugged/aimed at the ceiling; ask who reviews the DVR footage and how often.
Parking and dumpster area: no lighting, no camera coverage of the gate, evidence of illegal dumping.
Office: paper work-order log, a whiteboard of 'no heat' calls, a wall of keys, super's phone as the only alerting channel.

Ask three questions on site: 'how did you find out about the last water leak?', 'what happened on the last no-heat call, and did anyone document the temperature?', 'who looks at camera footage, and how long is it kept?' The answers are the sales pitch.

pilot.scope: One building, 20-60 units, 6 weeks elapsed (2 weeks install + 4 weeks monitored). Deliverables: (1) 15-25 leak/freeze sensors covering boiler room, water-entry/meter area, laundry, water heater closets, trash room and a sample of 4-6 units installed under lease language plus one-day notice; (2) 6-10 temperature sensors at boiler supply/return and in 4-6 representative apartments with a heat-log dashboard and exportable report keyed to the NJ 68/65F standard; (3) 3-4 PoE cameras on entrance, package area and parking with zone rules and human-verified alerts; (4) one local mini PC running Frigate + Home Assistant, remote-accessible to us only, cameras on an isolated VLAN; (5) written tenant notice and retention policy, plus a one-page runbook for the super.
pilot.hardware: About 20 Aqara-class Zigbee leak sensors ($18.99 each), 10 Zigbee temperature/humidity sensors plus a Zigbee coordinator, 4 Dahua/OEM 4MP PoE turrets ($219.99 each at a US reseller), 8-port PoE switch, Beelink EQ13-class N100 mini PC (~$200) with a 1-2 TB SSD and a small UPS, cabling, connectors and mounts. Boiler burner run-time via dry-contact relay or the existing control's Modbus port where available. Rough bill of materials: $2,000-$2,400 (mixes verified list prices for the sensors, cameras and Pi/N100 class parts with estimated prices for the switch, SSD, UPS and cabling, marked as inference).
pilot.success_metric: Commissioning test with a controlled leak and a controlled temperature drop: 100% of test events alerted to the designated phone in under 60 seconds, with the correct location string. Then, over 4 weeks: zero missed freeze/heat-failure events, medians alert-to-acknowledge under 10 minutes during staffed hours, false alerts under 1 per camera per day after the second tuning pass, and a documented before/after comparison of 'how the last three incidents were discovered' versus the monitored period. Secondary: owner-reported staff hours per week on rounds.
pilot.cost_range: $5,000-$10,500 installed for the pilot building. Arithmetic: hardware $2,000-$2,400 (above) + installation and commissioning 40-60 labor hours at $75-$125/hr ($3,000-$7,500) + $0-$500 cabling/misc and trip charges = $5,000 low end, $10,400 high end. Ongoing monitoring and maintenance quoted at $250-$500/month for the pilot building (inference: 2-4 service hours per month plus a share of remote infrastructure). Benchmarks: Rhombus lists an R200 at $599 + a $149 Professional license = $748 MSRP total, with no license term stated and AI features not included at that tier; a Verkada CD22 alone is $799 MSRP before its required (unpublished-price) license; Runwise ran $14,375/yr for a 349-unit heating program.
pilot.assumptions: Assumes the building is within 30 minutes of Milltown, the landlord will use the N.J.A.C. 5:10-1.2 maintenance-access route with one-day notice (and lease language) for in-unit sensors, there is power and a network drop in the boiler room, the boiler has an accessible dry contact or readable control, cameras can be cabled (no WiFi-only cameras), and the owner supplies one responsive on-site contact. Excludes electrical work, boiler repairs, asbestos/lead disturbance, and any permitting. Does not assume an insurance premium reduction - no NJ insurer credit was confirmed. Labor rates are our own estimate; no local contractor quote was obtained.

fit_score.rationale: Demand is real and partly quantified: water damage and freezing is the second-largest homeowners loss category (22.6% of 2023 losses, $15,400 average severity 2019-2023), package theft is a documented $16B problem in 2024, and NJ's 68F/65F heat rule makes boiler monitoring a compliance product, not a nice-to-have - but the multifamily-specific severity figure I most wanted (a commercial real-estate average claim) could not be confirmed, so demand is 15 not higher (of 20). Buyers are abundant in Middlesex County (dense pre-1950 rental stock plus a long tail of small management firms) though I could not pull county establishment counts, hence 11 of 15. Ability to pay is the constraint (10 of 15): small owners are capital-poor and enterprise per-camera pricing sets a price anchor - $399-$3,299 per Rhombus camera plus a $149-$649 license, or $799 MSRP for a Verkada CD22 before its unpublished license - which makes a $5-10.5k install a hard sell, and note the $748 Rhombus R200 figure buys video/cloud storage, not AI analytics. Technical feasibility is the strongest axis (17 of 20): Frigate publishes concrete detector latencies on exactly the hardware we would use, leak sensors cost $18.99, and the whole stack runs locally, with retrofit wiring as the main unknown. Legal risk is moderate but manageable (11 of 15): no NJ statute found banning common-area landlord cameras, one-party consent for audio, a clear maintenance-access route (one-day notice) plus a hard consent rule for anything beyond inspection inside a unit, and face recognition/LPR-enforcement avoidable. Defensibility is weakest (9 of 15): the models are free, the hardware is commodity, so the moat is installation quality, nuisance-alert tuning and integration with the owner's work-order system - a services moat, not a technology moat. Sub-scores sum to 73 of 100.

risks: Price anchor problem: Verkada/Rhombus per-camera hardware and licenses, and enterprise per-unit monitoring, set expectations that make a $5-10.5k pilot feel expensive to a 40-unit owner with a high deductible.

Alert fatigue destroys the product faster than missed detections: laundry humidity, steam pipes, rain on a lens, and delivery drivers will generate false positives unless someone tunes zones and thresholds weekly for the first month.

In-unit sensors depend on process discipline, not just hardware: NJ allows maintenance access on about one day's notice under N.J.A.C. 5:10-1.2, but a tenant can still dispute entry, and anything beyond inspection/maintenance needs its own lease provision - a building with an adversarial tenant association may only support common-area coverage.

Liability exposure if an alert is missed or a person is misidentified - an owner may argue the monitoring service assumed the duty to catch it. Contracts need clear scope, disclaimers, and a human-verification step.
Insurance premium credits are unproven: no NJ insurer credit for leak sensors was confirmed, so ROI must stand on avoided damage, water bills and staff time.

Retrofit reality: pre-1950 brick buildings have thick walls (Zigbee range problems), undocumented risers, and boilers with proprietary or no digital controls; each site is a small custom job, which caps how fast this scales.
Hardware support risk: consumer sensors (Aqara-class) have no vendor SLA; a mixed-vendor stack means we own the failures.
Face recognition and enforcement-grade LPR invite biometric-privacy, fair-housing and defamation claims for marginal value - leave them out.
The large vendors are moving down-market with cheaper tiers and channel programs; a services-only moat can be undercut on price if they bundle installation.

Camera sourcing and pricing are volatile: Reolink and several US retail pages returned 404/403 during this check, so per-camera budgets may move and Frigate's own guidance favours Dahua/Hikvision over cheap 4K Reolink models.
caveats: Reliability differs sharply across the quantified claims. The water-loss share and severity come from ISO/Verisk via Triple-I and are solid for single-family homeowners policies; they exclude tenants and condo policies, and I could not confirm any multifamily-specific severity figure (the Gallagher commercial real-estate number is search-index-only, page unopenable). Package theft is a USPS OIG estimate with acknowledged reporting gaps, not a census.
